indian-startups-cac89b312c.headline: India needs its own AI safety framework, not a copy of US pact: Industry experts
indian-startups-cac89b312c.fulltext:
[Text below is BusinessLine's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
India needs to develop an AI safety and governance framework tailored to its own languages, use cases, and scale of deployment, even as it aligns with global standards, as the country seeks to build indigenous AI capabilities while remaining one of the world’s largest markets for AI deployment, industry players said.
On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump announced that technology executives had agreed to establish voluntary AI standards following a meeting with industry leaders. Under the agreement, companies would work with “independent auditors” to assess whether their AI systems operate as intended. They also committed to ensuring that their AI tools do not “hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.”
Dr. Amit Sheth, Founding Director, Indian AI Research Organisation (IAIRO), explained that voluntary industry commitments can be useful in establishing a common baseline for responsible AI development. They can encourage companies to adopt practices such as pre-deployment testing, red-teaming, documentation, incident reporting, and ongoing monitoring before these become mandatory requirements.
Auditor Access
Meanwhile, Prof. Ganesh Ramakrishnan, founding director of BharatGen, noted that the effectiveness of audits depends on the access provided to auditors, making it important to build trust and oversight into AI systems from the outset rather than treating them as an afterthought.
BharatGen is a government-funded initiative developing foundational multimodal AI models for India’s linguistic and cultural diversity.
He also stressed the importance of provenance and auditability, which can support AI sovereignty and transparency for countries, build trust for businesses using AI in regulated sectors, and help individuals understand how their data was used.
“For India, I expect the path to look different, with a whole-of-government approach in which academia, industry, and public institutions build together. At BharatGen, we maintain provenance across our data pipeline so that it can be re-inspected, including for DPDP compliance. Making auditability practical at scale, and across our many languages and contexts, is where research has to play a key role.”
Building AI
Sheth said India should not simply replicate a framework developed for a different AI ecosystem.
“India’s AI journey is distinct. We are a large-scale adopter of AI and an emerging developer of indigenous AI capabilities. As India moves from primarily an AI services and deployment market towards a global AI product and research nation, safety needs to be built into the development of our own AI capabilities from the outset,” he shared.
Devyani Gupta, Co-Founder & CEO of Arrowhead AI, echoed that India’s pact should not simply be copied from the US.
“India’s AI story is also being written by companies that deploy AI at scale, not only by those training frontier models. An Indian pact should focus on how AI behaves when it reaches a customer: do they know they’re talking to an AI, did they consent, and who is accountable when something goes wrong? A voluntary pact lets Indian companies earn that trust before regulation has to demand it,” she said.
Indian Benchmarks
Gupta added that most of the AI risk Indian citizens face will come from deployment, not model training — an agent mis-selling a product, misreading a borrower’s intent, or serving a vernacular speaker worse than an English speaker.
Sheth also said AI models should disclose their capabilities, limitations and known risks before commercial deployment, especially when they could affect individuals or organisations. He added that developers should be responsible for the model’s training, capabilities, security and evaluation, while deployers should be accountable for how it is integrated, the data it uses and the impact of its outputs.
“India needs to develop the capability to conduct these evaluations ourselves. A model that performs well on a global benchmark may behave differently across Indian languages, domains and social contexts. Building Indian evaluation benchmarks, testing capabilities and safety expertise is therefore as important as building the models themselves,” he said.
Published on October 1, 2026

Trump names AI czar to head White House task force
October 4, 2026
US President Donald Trump has chosen members to lead a new AI task force to coordinate the administration's response to the rapidly evolving technology.
US President Donald Trump on Sunday announced a White House task force to coordinate the administration's response to artificial intelligence (AI).
The group will be led by director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon chief technology officer Emil Michael and director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor.
The task force, named the "Super Intelligence Force" or SI, in accordance with the term that the president prefers over AI.
"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies," Trump said in Truth Social post on Sunday.
Trump under pressure to regulate AI
Trump in September said he would create a new AI force to oversee the development of the fast-moving technology, but has so far opposed any strict regulation that codifies pillars of AI safety into law.
"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth of this incredible industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump said in the September post where he announced he was going to choose an AI czar.
Leading up to the midterm elections in November, Trump has been under pressure to address concerns about AI risks. AI researchers and tech CEOs have sounded the alarm about the existential threat that the technology can pose.
Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei, for example, published an essay last month in which he called for a global slowdown in the race to develop AI. His call was met with agreement from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Trump, AI CEOs sign safety pact
The US president hosted a White House lunch for nearly 20 tech titans at the end of September, where he said there was an agreement in the room that there should be "tremendous self-regulation" by tech companies.
The tech leaders signed onto a one-page document that relies on companies to voluntarily follow through on their safety commitments. But the accord is largely symbolic since it is not an official order.
